title: The communion of saints (CCC 946–962)
hook: the living, the dead being purified, and the saints, one family

segments.voice: Yesterday, other religions: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in them. Your line was nothing true is rejected. Today, a circle that crosses even death.

Walk into an old Catholic church and look up. On the walls, in the windows, painted on the ceiling: faces. Apostles, martyrs, a young nun from Normandy, a Polish priest, a mother, a beggar. Now look down at the pews: a retired nurse, a kid on a phone, a man who comes every day since his wife died. And somewhere, the Church says, his wife too. Catholics see the painted faces, the people in the pews and the dead they love as one gathering. There's a line in the Creed that says so.
screen: `FACES ON THE WALLS.` → `PEOPLE IN THE PEWS.` → `ONE GATHERING.`

segments.voice: The Apostles' Creed says: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints. Catholics say it at the start of the rosary, and promise it again at every baptism. In Latin it's communio sanctorum, and sanctorum can mean holy people or holy things. The Catechism says both are true: a sharing in holy things, above all the Eucharist, the sacraments, the faith, and a sharing among holy people. That one family of God, it says, exists in three states at once. Some are pilgrims on earth. Some have died and are being purified. And some are in glory, seeing God. Death doesn't cut the family in three. It's one family in three rooms. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the living as runners in a race, with "so great a cloud of witnesses over our head": the faithful of the chapter before, who bore witness by their lives, now all around the runners. And Catholics believe love and prayer pass between the rooms in every direction. The saints in heaven pray for those on earth; that's why Catholics ask them for help, the way you'd ask a friend to pray for you. The living pray for the dead who are being purified. And the good done by any member, the Catechism says, helps all the others.
screen: `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · `HOLY THINGS, AND HOLY PEOPLE.` · `ONE FAMILY IN THREE STATES.` · `PRAYER GOES EVERY DIRECTION.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you loved who has died, a grandparent, a friend, a parent, someone you barely knew but think of; say their name quietly and remember one ordinary thing about them, a laugh, a phrase, the way they made coffee. If you pray, you can pray for them now, in your own words or with the old line, eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. If you don't, hold them in love for a minute.
Communio sanctorum, the Latin behind the communion of saints: a sharing in holy things, and among holy people, living, dead and in glory. Today's word.

Your line: one family. The week ran from dignity to misericordia, soma christou, the four marks, other Christians, other religions, and now a family that death doesn't break. Day three hundred twenty-two: another week, done.

`DAY 322 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MARY, MOTHER OF THE CHURCH.`

howItsDone: Catholics profess the communion of saints in the Apostles' Creed, ask the saints to pray for them, pray for the dead at every Mass, and keep All Saints on November 1 and All Souls on November 2.

original.note: Latin: the communion of saints, or of holy things. the Creed means both.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saints are a separate club of perfect people.
what it means: one family of all the faithful, living, being purified, and in glory, sharing holy things and prayer.
what a scholar hears: sanctorum as masculine and neuter genitive; the Apostles' Creed; CCC 954's three states; Hebrews 12:1.

notes: Apostles' Creed line from the Book of Common Prayer 1662 and Douay-Rheims Hebrews 12:1 given from memory; confirm wording and capitalization.
The practice offers the opening of the traditional prayer 'Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord' (Requiem aeternam); a real prayer, not a new one. Confirm wording.
CCC 946–962 paraphrased (holy things and holy people; three states in CCC 954; intercession of saints in CCC 956). Confirm.
Many Protestants profess the communion of saints in the Creed but do not ask saints to intercede; not raised today.

Audit (second sample): 'a teenage girl from Normandy' fit no obvious saint (Thérèse of Lisieux was from Normandy but died at 24; Joan of Arc was from Lorraine, though burned at Rouen) and is now 'a young nun from Normandy'. The Creed line was quoted from the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, an odd source on the Catholic path; it is now given in the plain Catholic wording without a quotation, with a note that Catholics say it at the start of the rosary and in the baptismal promises. 'Watching and cheering' read Hebrews 12:1 as spectators; it now follows the text, where the witnesses are the faithful of Hebrews 11 who bore witness.
